To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the Itkillik Yedoma exposure provides a continuous paleoenvironmental record covering the entire period prior to the LGM in northern Alaska, 2) Middle Wisconsinian climate was 1–2°C cooler than today, and 3) Late Wisconsinian climate was characterized by grassland vegetation, 2–3°C cooler than today and more arid conditions.
the Middle Wisconsinan climate was warm enough for peat formation and the Late Wisconsinian climate was too cold for peat formation.

the climate in northern Alaska became colder and drier at the end of the Middle Wisconsinan and remained so until the beginning of the Late Wisconsinan, with a short warming event around 30 cal ky BP, followed by a gradual cooling trend.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the climate of interior Alaska and Yukonia during the Middle Wisconsin was warmer than today, and that the Late Wisconsinan (Last Glacial Maximum) was colder than the present.
the climate in northern Alaska was 1–2 °C cooler and drier than the present during the Middle Wisconsinian interstadial, while 2–3 °C cooler and 10% drier than today during the Late Wisconsinian.
the climate of the Middle to Late Wisconsinan in northern Alaska was colder and more arid than today, and the vegetation was more diverse than in the modern environment.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Itkillik yedoma provides a unique record of the environmental changes that occurred in the Arctic during the last glacial period.

the Itkillik yedoma exposure is a valuable archive of Middle to Late Wisconsinan paleoclimate and paleoenvironmental changes in northern Alaska, and it can serve as a proxy for the paleoclimate and vegetation history of the Beringia region.
the Middle Wisconsinan interstadial was characterized by a warm, moist climate, with a vegetation cover dominated by grassland.
